title: Igbu Ịchị — the festival of the renewal of the oath
description: Held once every seven years: seven days, seven Uniku, and the renewal of the oath the ancestors took to become Ide. The Great Day, the homage, the procession, the Acts of Service in place of sacrifices.
html:
IGBU ỊCHỊ

The Great Festival of the Renewal of the Oath

Festival Charter and Programme · Held once every seven years

Ide gathers around the Ikala, who stands for the living and the dead, and renews the oath its ancestors took to become Ide.

At a glance

Cycle

Once every seven years; seven days; seven Uniku

Heart of the festival

Homage to the Ikala, and the renewal of the oath the ancestors took to become Ide

Who gathers

Representatives of every Obo and every Uniku (Ulide, Ezeme, Oyiora, Dilibe, Oviaeli, Anaka, Akuana), the Iyi, the Nde Ako, elders, age-grades, riders, titled women and men, and the people

The Great Day

The Ikala’s procession, the Great Homage, the Renewal of the Oath, the Creed, the Acts of Service, then the Procession of Inherited Gold

Core rule

In place of sacrifices, the community performs works of service

Status

Draft 2, October 2026. Ide names are marked “provisional” for your language canon to settle.

1. What Igbu Ịchị is

Igbu Ịchị is the renewal of the oath. Long ago the ancestors took an oath and by it became Ide. Every seven years the living Ide gather in the capital to take that same oath again, in the presence of the ones who first took it. The ceremony tells every Ide person that they are not a new people. They are the same people, still bound by the same word, and they will keep it and stand stronger than ever.

The Ikala at the centre

The Ikala is the living point where the nation and its ancestors meet. He is half human and half spirit, a living god who stands for the living Ide and for the dead Ide together. Paying homage to him is therefore paying homage to the whole nation across time: the ancestors who made the oath, the people who keep it now, and the generations still to come.

For this reason the whole festival is arranged around him. Every group that rides, parades, sings or serves does so to bring itself before the Ikala and renew its place in the oath.

Principles

  • The oath is the point. Every display, however grand, leads to a renewal of loyalty, service or remembrance.
  • The living and the dead are both present. The ancestors are not remembered from a distance. They are carried into the procession and addressed in the oath.
  • Service replaces sacrifice. No animal or blood sacrifice is part of Igbu Ịchị. The community offers labour, trees, public works and gifts instead.
  • Every Uniku and Obo has a place. No group only watches; each rides, parades, performs or serves.
  • Women and men take part as equals in rank. Both are titled in Ide society, so women and men ride, parade, take the oath and recite the Creed together. The gold procession is an added women’s institution, not their only place in the festival.
  • Honour by merit, not cost. Prizes go to unity, craft, preservation and service, never to the most expensive display.
  • Ide in every detail. Dress, ranks, horses, music, words and symbols all come from Ide custom and the Ide language canon.

2. The Ikala’s procession

Ide has a horse culture, and the Ikala’s procession is its highest expression. It is a mounted procession through the capital in which the whole nation rides before the Ikala and the Ikala arrives last, so that everyone has gone ahead to meet him. It moves slowly and in order. Each company has one meaning and one task.

Order of the procession

From front to back:

#

Company (provisional names)

Who and what

1

The Heralds and Drummers

Horn-blowers, drummers and criers on foot and on horseback. They announce each company and clear the way.

2

The Seven Banners

One banner-bearer for each Uniku, mounted. Their banners show the seven Uniku to the people and to the Ikala.

3

The Vanguard

The seven Uniku troops, 15 to 25 riders each, women and men, in their own heritage dress. They ride in formation.

4

The Riding Houses

Families who keep horses across generations and have earned a recorded place in the procession.

5

The Age-Grade Companies

Age-grades in matching dress, mounted and on foot, behind their banners.

6

The Keepers of the Oath

Sworn bearers of the Ọkwa Ugo and Ọkwa Nza, carried upright before the Ikala.

7

The Nde Ako and the Iyi

The council and the Iyi, mounted, in their ranks of title, women and men together.

8

The Ancestral Company

Led by the Anaka. Bearers carry the emblems of the ancestors, with a seat set apart for the first Ide who took the oath. Before the Ikala rides the Seat of the Ancestors, so the dead enter the capital with him.

9

The Ikala

Mounted on his own horse, in ceremonial regalia, shaded and flanked by attendants. He appears last, as the one to whom the whole procession is moving.

10

The Household of the Ikala

His attendants, singers and the keepers of his regalia.

11

The Rearguard

A mounted guard drawn from the Oviaeli. It closes the procession, keeps order and secures the route.

The Ikala’s horse

The Ikala rides a horse set aside for him alone. It is raised and trained across the seven-year cycle by a designated riding house, given a name, and ridden by no one else. At the end of the cycle the horse is honoured and retired, and the next horse is chosen.

Dress and regalia (proposals)

  • Each Uniku rides in its own heritage colours and cloth. The seven together should read as one nation.
  • The Ikala’s regalia is the richest on the field and carries the marks of both the living and the ancestral line. The Ide canon should define the cloth, beads, crown or headpiece and the colours.
  • Horses carry matching cloth and ornament in the colours of their Uniku or house. Horse gear follows each company’s heritage and is not ranked by cost.
  • Gold is worn by those who hold it by inheritance or title. It is not required of any rider.

The route

The procession moves from the assembly ground, through the quarters of the capital that hold historic families and ancestral places, and ends at the forecourt before the Ikala’s seat. The people line the route. At the forecourt each company halts in its place, and the Great Homage begins.

3. The seven days

The festival moves from arrival, through the powers and memory of the nation, to the Great Day. Seven days matches the seven Uniku and the seven-year cycle.

Day

Name (provisional)

What happens

1

The Gathering

Delegations from every Obo and Uniku enter the capital behind their banners and are received and housed. Horses are stabled and inspected. The Ikala withdraws into seclusion, where he is not seen and prepares in the presence of the ancestors.

2

Day of Elders and Masquerades

Elders, women and men, are seated in places of honour and their counsel is received. Senior masquerades appear and perform under their own custom. The elders restate the customs Ide will keep for the next seven years.

3

Day of Ancestors

Rites of remembrance at the ancestral places. The names of the ancestors are recited. The two Ọkwa are brought out for the sword rites. The chiefs and Uniku heads give a public account of how they kept their trust.

4

Day of Age-Grades

Each age-grade parades in its matching dress behind its banner and renders its homage as a group. Riding houses are named and recognised.

5

Day of the Horse

Each Uniku troop rides its full display before the people: the charge, the halt in line and the salute. Judged for unity, timing, dress and horse care. The procession is rehearsed.

6

Eve of Renewal

A night of vigil. Disputes between groups are brought to the Nde Ako so that no one carries a grievance into the oath. Families lay out their inherited gold and records.

7

The Great Day

The Ikala’s procession, the Great Homage, the Renewal of the Oath, the Creed, the Acts of Service and the Procession of Inherited Gold (section 4).

4. The Great Day

Time

Rite

What takes place

Dawn

Assembly

The companies form up in the order of the procession. Banners are raised.

Morning

The Ikala Emerges

The seven days of seclusion end. The Ikala emerges in full regalia, the Seat of the Ancestors is placed before him, and the procession begins to move.

Late morning

The Procession and the Great Homage

The procession reaches the forecourt (section 2). Each company renders homage in turn (see below).

Midday

The Renewal of the Oath

The ancestors’ oath is stated. The Ikala renews it first, standing for the living and the dead. Then the Iyi, the Nde Ako and all titled leaders, women and men, then the people (see below).

Midday

The Recitation of the Creed

The whole assembly recites the Civic Creed in unison.

Afternoon

The Acts of Service

In place of sacrifices, the community performs tangible good works: planting trees, building public works and donating to the National Trust. Gifts go directly to people experiencing poverty.

Late afternoon

to sunset

The Procession of Inherited Gold

The women’s procession passes before the Ikala and closes the ceremony (section 8).

Night

Blessing and Feast

The Ikala blesses the people. A communal feast follows. The Seven-Year Ledger is sealed and the next cycle is declared.

The Great Homage

Homage is paid by the group, not the individual. Each company comes forward in the order of the procession and follows the same form:

  • Approach. The company advances at a walk and halts in a straight line before the Ikala. Riders in the Vanguard may end with a short charge and a sudden halt.
  • Salute. The company’s leader raises the signal of the Uniku, Obo or age-grade, and all members salute together.
  • Declaration. The leader names the company and the ancestors of its line and declares that it comes to renew its place in the oath. An English placeholder: “We are of Ide. Our fathers and mothers took the oath. We have kept it, and we keep it.” The Ide wording is for your canon.
  • Reply. The Ikala, or a bearer for him, answers with a blessing. The company withdraws to its place.

When all companies have rendered homage, the whole assembly turns toward the Ikala together and the closing salute is given.

The Renewal of the Oath

  • The Anaka, as keepers of teaching and memory, state the oath of the ancestors and name those who first took it.
  • The Ikala renews the oath first, as the one who stands for the living and the dead. In doing so he renews it for the ancestors as well as the nation.
  • The Iyi, the Nde Ako, and all titled leaders, women and men, reaffirm their oath to the Covenant before the Nde Ako and the people.
  • Then the people take the oath together, and move directly into the Recitation of the Creed.

Why this order. The oath comes before the gold because order comes first. The Acts of Service come before the gold so wealth is displayed only after the community has given. The women’s procession then reads as the fruit of a renewed oath.

5. The Ọkwa and the rites of remembrance

The Ide ceremonial swords, the Ọkwa Ugo and the Ọkwa Nza, carry the festival’s ancestral and royal rites. They are borne by sworn Keepers of the Oath and appear in the sword rites on Day 3 and in the procession and oath on the Great Day.

Proposed roles for the two swords

These are proposals. Please correct them against your canon, since I do not want to invent symbolism for objects you have already defined.

  • Ọkwa Ugo (proposed): the sword of sovereignty. Carried before the Ikala and used for the rites of renewal and blessing.
  • Ọkwa Nza (proposed): the sword of covenant and service. Carried at the oath and raised at the Acts of Service.

The rites

  • Remembrance of Ancestors (Day 3). Offerings of kola, palm wine and water, the recital of ancestral names, and a sword dance by the sworn bearers. Rites follow Ide religious custom and the teaching of the Anaka. The sacred part is by custom, not obligation.
  • Renewal of the Ikala. In seclusion the Ikala reviews the seven years past in the presence of the ancestors. On the Great Day he re-appears as renewed in office and takes the oath first.
  • Account of Stewardship. Chiefs and Uniku heads give a short public account of what they did with their trust over the seven years.
  • The Blessing. At the closing feast the Ikala blesses the people with an emblem of renewal, a leaf, plant or other sign of Ide’s choosing.

6. The Uniku troops

Each of the seven Uniku fields one troop of 15 to 25 riders, women and men, in its own heritage dress. They form the Vanguard of the Ikala’s procession and ride the full display on Day 5.

Element

Design

Troop

15 to 25 riders per Uniku, led by a troop leader. Dress, colours and banner belong to the Uniku.

The charge

Riders line up, gather speed together, charge about 300 metres, and halt abruptly in one straight line before the Ikala, then raise the salute.

The volley

One simultaneous ceremonial discharge at the halt. Blank charges only, with licensed handlers (section 11).

Judging

Unity and timing of the charge, fidelity of dress and heritage, and horse condition and welfare. Not the cost of the horse or garments.

Riding houses

Families that keep horses and train riders across generations are named and recognised publicly.

Women and men

Women and men ride together in every troop, since both are titled in Ide society.

7. Elders, masquerades and age-grades

The Day of Elders and Masquerades

This day makes the nation’s social authority visible and honours those who carry the nation’s memory.

  • Seating of the elders. The oldest women and men of each Obo are seated in places of honour and their counsel is formally received.
  • Procession of senior masquerades. Large and senior masks from each Obo process under custom, with their own custodians. The masks keep their rules, initiations and secrecy.
  • Ceremonial performance. Each Obo presents one performance: dance, drum or mask. Judging looks to craft and fidelity to local custom.
  • Declaration of custom. The elders publicly restate the customs Ide will keep for the next seven years.

The Age-Grade Parade

People are grouped by age-grade. Each grade agrees its attire and colours months ahead and parades behind its banner.

  • Each age-grade pays homage to the Ikala as a group, not as individuals.
  • Groups are open to women and men regardless of wealth, and recognised for turnout, organisation, dress and service done in the previous seven years.
  • Age-grades are the main organisers of the Acts of Service work teams on the Great Day.

8. The Procession of Inherited Gold

The women’s gathering closes Igbu Ịchị. Gold is already part of everyday Ide identity and dress. This is not a new gold culture. It is a once-in-seven-years occasion where women publicly display their wealth, family gold and the heirlooms inherited from mothers and grandmothers, passing before the Ikala as the ancestors’ line passes before him.

What it celebrates

  • Wealth: gold and other valued heirlooms a woman owns.
  • Inheritance: pieces passed between grandmothers, mothers, daughters and granddaughters.
  • Prestige: the finest jewellery worn with ceremonial attire.
  • Continuity: proof that each generation has preserved what the last gave it.

How it runs

Stage

What happens

Assembly of women

Women from all seven Uniku assemble in prescribed ceremonial attire (wrappers, beads, head ties, gold ornaments), with special dress conventions for titled women where they apply. Each group stands under its Uniku banner.

Display of family gold

Necklaces, bracelets, earrings, rings, waist ornaments, coins and other heirlooms are shown. Women choose which pieces to display.

Presentation of heirlooms

Families present significant pieces and tell their history: who owned it, how it was acquired, how it passed down.

Generations together

Grandmothers, mothers, daughters and granddaughters stand side by side. Newly married women, young adults and senior women each have a place.

Before the Ikala

The procession passes before the Ikala. As a proposal, he blesses the inherited gold in the name of the ancestors who first wore it.

Recognition

Recognition goes to exceptional heirlooms, preservation, craftsmanship and the historical value of a collection.

The Gift of Gold

Voluntary. Women or families may give a gold piece or its value to the National Trust, honoured publicly but never required, tying the procession to the Acts of Service.

The Seven-Year Ledger

Each family keeps a ledger across the seven years: what was added, inherited, gifted or passed on since the last Igbu Ịchị. It is brought to the procession, so the display shows continuity and growth, not just ownership. A small piece with a well-kept history can carry as much honour as a large, recent collection.

Provenance and the optional gold institutions

The gold bank and the school stay behind the culture and work between ceremonies. They are optional for every woman.

  • Gold custody and records: secure storage between cycles, independent assay of purity and weight, valuation and optional documentation of provenance.
  • Gold-backed loans: voluntary. Loans are valued on pure-gold content (for example, 22-karat jewellery is 91.67% pure), with a conservative loan-to-value limit, written contracts, no hidden fees and a fair process for overdue loans.
  • Ide School of Gold and Precious Metals: teaches purity, valuation, craftsmanship, provenance, finance and trade, with three voluntary levels: Gold Literate, Gold Steward and Gold Professional.

Rules that protect women and families

  • Women own their gold. Marriage, widowhood or family seniority never transfers it to a husband, in-laws or clan.
  • Every woman has a place. No minimum amount of gold is needed to take part, and there is no gold requirement for marriage.
  • No woman must borrow or deposit gold in order to participate.
  • Display is selective. The value and location of full holdings stay private, and security is provided on the day.
  • A documented modest heirloom ranks alongside a costly one.
  • Gold from theft, forced labour or unlawful mining is not recognised.

9. Who runs what

Each Uniku leads the part of the festival closest to its established responsibilities. These are institutional roles and do not restrict who can take part.

Uniku

Existing focus

Festival responsibility

Ulide

Art and Culture

Regalia and procession design, exhibitions, staging of the gold procession and the Day of Elders and Masquerades.

Ezeme

Wealth and Enterprise

Festival finance, the National Trust gift drive, the gold bank and appraisal network, sponsorship rules.

Oyiora

Politics and Leadership

Protocol, the order of homage, the oath ceremony and public accountability.

Dilibe

Science and Health

Medical teams, food and water safety, horse veterinary care, assay testing for gold.

Oviaeli

Military and Law

The Rearguard, security, safe handling of ceremonial arms, crowd control, legal rights of owners and exhibitors.

Anaka

Priesthood and Teaching

The Ancestral Company, the oath’s statement, the Creed’s instruction, ethical teaching and historical records.

Akuana

Agriculture and Environment

Stables, fodder, tree-planting sites, environmental standards and responsible sourcing for gold.

10. The seven-year preparation cycle

Year

Work

After the festival

Seal the Seven-Year Ledger. Announce the next cycle. Publish what the Acts of Service achieved. Retire the Ikala’s horse and begin choosing the next.

Years 1 to 2

Review what worked. Form and register new age-grades. Begin family heirloom records with permission.

Years 3 to 4

Build the riding programme: riding houses, stables, training grounds and horse welfare standards. Open the Gold School’s first classes.

Years 5 to 6

Commission regalia and banners. Prepare the Acts of Service project list with the National Trust. Rehearse the oath and the Creed.

Year 7

Final rehearsals, logistics and security planning. Seven days of festival. The Great Day.

11. Safety, welfare and legal safeguards

  • Ceremonial firearms. Rifle volleys require lawful licensing and permits. Use blank charges only, trained and licensed handlers, controlled firing lanes and spectator distance. If permits cannot be obtained, replace the volley with a drum and horn salute.
  • Horse welfare. Veterinary checks before and after each ride, shade, water, rest rules, limits on gallop runs per horse, and no horse competes while injured or lame.
  • The Ikala’s safety. A trained rearguard, a controlled route and a calm, schooled horse. The Ikala’s horse is never ridden by anyone else.
  • Crowd safety. Barriers, marshals, medical posts, clear routes and capacity limits at the forecourt and for the gold procession.
  • Masquerades. Masks stay under the custom of their own Obo. The festival does not publish or expose their secrets.
  • Faith inclusion. Sacred rites follow Ide religious custom and are by participation, not compulsion. Civic rites are open to everyone.
  • Gold security. Secure display areas, discreet identity checks and insurance where available, with no public listing of valuables.
  • Environment. Tree-planting uses native species, with waste and noise limits across the seven days.

12. Decisions that are yours

  • Ide names. The names for the seven days, the troops, the companies of the procession, the Ikala’s seclusion and the gold procession.
  • The Ikala’s regalia. Cloth, beads, headpiece and colours, and what marks him as living and ancestral at once.
  • Roles of the Ọkwa. Confirm or correct the proposed roles of the Ọkwa Ugo and Ọkwa Nza.
  • The oath’s words. The text of the ancestors’ oath, the homage declaration and the Creed’s place within it.
  • Iyi and Nde Ako. I used these titles only as you described them. Add their precise duties if you want them to lead specific rites.
  • Length of seclusion. Seven days is a design choice matching the cycle.

Appendix: where the ideas came from

The festival above is written as an Ide institution. These are the existing traditions that informed its structure, with what I could confirm by search and what I could not.

Tradition

What informed Igbu Ịchị

What the sources confirm

Tbourida / Fantasia

(Morocco)

The Uniku troops: formation gallop, halt in a line, ceremonial volley, each troop carrying its own heritage.

Troops (sorba) gallop and fire together and halt in a line. UNESCO-listed. Women ride today. Reported troop sizes vary (six or more in Morocco, 9 to 11 in Algerian groups), so 15 to 25 is your design choice.

Durbar

(Northern Nigeria)

The mounted procession of the ruler with regiments, and homage from the leaders of the quarters.

The Emir parades with horsemen, musicians and regiments; district heads pay homage and reaffirm loyalty. Kano’s Durbar runs in stages and ends with a salute at the palace gate.

Igue / Ugie

(Benin Kingdom)

Ancestral rites, sword rites, the chiefs’ account of stewardship and the public blessing.

The Oba honours royal ancestors at altars, performs sword dances for forebears and blesses the people. Igue includes animal sacrifice, which Igbu Ịchị replaces with the Acts of Service.

Ojude Oba

(Ijebu-Ode)

Homage by group, age-grade parades in matching dress and recognition of riding houses.

Age-grades (regberegbe) parade and horse-riding families ride before the Awujale. Outfits are agreed months ahead.

Olojo

(Ile-Ife)

The ruler’s seclusion and single appearance.

The Ooni withdraws into seclusion (reports say five to seven days) and appears once a year in the Aare crown, accompanied by a gun salute.

Ime Ntụ

(Nkpor)

The Day of Elders and Masquerades.

Not confirmed. Wikipedia lists “Ntu” among Nkpor’s traditional festivals, but I found no source describing it. Idemili North is widely noted for large masquerades such as Ijele and Agaba, and masquerades commonly uphold elders’ authority. The details here come from your description. Please confirm with Nkpor elders.

Desfile da Mordomia

(Viana do Castelo, Portugal)

The idea of women displaying family gold.

Women wear traditional dress and family gold in the procession. A widely cited figure of about 250 kg dates from 2013 and is not a verified figure for 2026. The Ide procession is built on the Uniku, Ide dress, inheritance custom and a seven-year cycle, and is not a copy.
